text: This five-dollar coffee could end up costing forty.
Not because of the café.
Because of your bank.
Imagine you have a hundred dollars.
You buy coffee for five, lunch for twelve, gas for twenty-eight, and groceries for ninety.
That’s thirty-five dollars more than you have.
Process those purchases in order, and only the last one causes an overdraft.
But Wells Fargo used to do something different.
It processed the biggest purchases first.
Groceries: ninety dollars.
Ten dollars left.
Gas? Overdraft.
Lunch? Another.
And that five-dollar coffee?
One more.
Same purchases. Same amount spent.
But THREE overdraft fees instead of one.
At thirty-five dollars per fee, that’s a hundred and five dollars in charges.
And that five-dollar coffee gets its own thirty-five-dollar fee.
Five becomes forty.
Court records describe a customer who went just a hundred and twenty dollars over — and incurred five hundred and six dollars in fees.
After years of appeals, a two-hundred-and-three-million-dollar restitution award was upheld in the case.
This was Wells Fargo’s old system.
The coffee was still five dollars.
The bank just made the order more expensive.
